#6140. Can You Redeem Airline Miles For Others? Yes, With Some Caveats

While I love redeeming miles & points for an amazing first or business class flight, one thing that brings me even more joy is being able to do that for friends & family. Along those lines, in this post I’d like to talk about which airline loyalty programs allow you to redeem your points for others. In a separate post, I addressed the topic of whether you can redeem hotel points for others.

While there are some areas where airline loyalty programs are stingy, the ability to redeem miles for others isn’t among those. Generally speaking, airline loyalty programs will let you redeem your miles for anyone you’d like (I’ll note some exceptions below, but unless otherwise noted, that’s what you should expect).

You can almost always do this directly through your frequent flyer program account, by just entering the name of the traveler during the booking process.

Now, it’s important to emphasize that this is for situations where you truly want to gift your rewards to others. Bartering airline miles violates the policies of virtually any airline loyalty program, and your account could be suspended and ticket could be forfeited if you’re caught doing this (and airline auditing departments are quite savvy).

So if you are going to redeem your airline miles for others, make sure you do so in good faith, without expecting anything in return.

To make things as easy as possible, I’d recommend that the person redeeming miles be the one to make the booking, rather than the person being redeemed for. Admittedly the policies do vary by airline:

If you’re making your reservation online, you can always just share your account number and password with someone to make a booking, though that does potentially pose a risk if you can’t fully trust the person (in which case you probably also shouldn’t share miles with them, come and think of it).

I won’t break that down by airline, since there are so many different policies, they sometimes change, and phone agents also often interpret them differently. However, the best way to go about this is to have the person with the miles make the booking. Just make sure you have the full, correct passport or travel document details for the traveler, so that the name matches the ID that will be presented at the time of travel.

There are hundreds of airline loyalty programs out there, and a vast majority of them will allow you to redeem your miles for anyone you’d like. There are some exceptions, though, as some airlines either limit the number of people you can redeem your miles for, or limit the types of people you can redeem your miles for (for example, direct family members).

Most of the programs restricting who you can redeem for are based in Asia. Let me note some of the most common programs with restrictions below. I’d like to emphasize, though, that this list is by no means exhaustive, so if I’ve missed any major programs, please do let me know.

Let me also mention that this is all about the program you book through, rather than the airline you travel with. For example, while All Nippon Airways Mileage Club has restrictions, you could book an award on All Nippon Airways through a partner program without being subjected to these rules.

There are airlines with just a few airplanes that have loyalty programs, so I’ll be focusing on “major” airlines, which I’ll define as airlines with 50+ planes. With that in mind, below are some of the major programs with restrictions:

With some programs that have these restrictions, you simply have to state what the relationship is between the person redeeming and the traveler. In other situations, you may have to provide proof of that relationship.

In some situations this gets tricky, like if we’re talking about same sex relationships that are recognized in some countries, but not others. For example, Korean Air SkyPass will accept same sex relationships as family if they’re recognized in a foreign country (and there’s documentation to prove it). However, since the South Korean government doesn’t legally recognize same sex relationships, a couple in the country wouldn’t be considered family for these purposes, unless they have a legally recognized relationship abroad.

With a vast majority of airline loyalty programs, you’re free to redeem your miles for friends & family without many restrictions. The best practice is to have the person redeeming the miles out of their account make the reservation.

There are a limited number of airline loyalty programs that limit who you can redeem your miles for. In some cases you’re limited to redeeming miles for direct family members, while in some cases you just have to specify redemption nominees, limiting the overall number of people you can redeem for.

What has your experience been with redeeming airline miles for others?

#6139. Air France Jet Turns Toward American Airlines Plane After Takeoff At LAX—Controller Warns ‘Traffic 12 O’Clock’

An Air France Airbus A350 turned left toward an American Airlines jet after takeoff from LAX early Saturday morning, requiring urgent intervention. The controller ordered Air France to turn immediately, and told American to return to 2,000 feet. He warned: “Traffic twelve o’clock. Less than a mile.” The incident is strikingly similar to another close call at the same airport almost exactly a year earlier. Air France Turned Toward The American Plane Both flights took off around 12:15 a.m. on November 7: Air France flight 28, an Airbus A350-900 registered F-HUVK, was departing runway 24L for Papeete, Tahiti. American Airlines flight 1660, an Airbus A321 registered N191UW, was departing runway 25R for Dallas–Fort Worth. These are parallel runways on opposite sides of the airport. Air France was supposed to head west over the ocean, but it began turning left – toward the departure path from the southern runway complex. Controller audio and flight tracking replay “Air France zero two eight heavy. Fly heading of two seven zero immediately.” That means turn west, to a compass heading of 270 degrees. Here’s the warning to American: “Traffic twelve o’clock. Less than a mile. Maintain two thousand.” American had already climbed above the altitude the controller wanted it to hold. The controller had to turn Air France away while bringing American back down to 2,000 feet. The FAA departure instructions in effect that day direct aircraft leaving runway 24L to begin on a heading of 251 degrees, proceed DLREY followed by ENNEY. The route continues broadly west. The Air France A350 shouldn’t have made an early left turn into the other departure stream. The controller had told Air France to “climb via” its assigned departure. That means following the published route and its altitude restrictions. He challenged the crew about turning to a heading, and repeatedly asked which departure they’d been instructed to fly. “Air France zero two eight heavy. Thank you very much. Possible pilot deviation. I have a number for you to call when you’re ready.” Air France flew a turn that didn’t match its assigned departure, and it’s not clear yet what happened: a wrong route loaded into the flight computer? a manually selected heading? a misunderstanding in the cockpit? How Close Was This? Simple Flying emphasizes 400 feet of vertical separation. But there was nearly a mile between the two planes. This was serious. Two departing aircraft had converging paths, the controller issued a traffic alert, and ordered an immediate turn while restricting the other aircraft’s altitude. But they didn’t come within 400 feet of colliding. I haven’t seen it reported that there was a collision avoidance resolution advisory. The departure route wasn’t followed, and the cockpit checksprevent the deviation from developing into a traffic conflict. The controller saw the conflict, issued instructions to prevent a problem, and both crews followed those instructions. Almost The Same Thing Happened Last Year On October 31, 2025, an ITA Airways Airbus A330neo departing Los Angeles for Rome turned left toward an American Airlines Airbus A321 bound for New York. It was the same pair of runways with ITA departing 24L, and American departing 25R. The controller ordered ITA right to heading 270 and told American to stop its climb at 1,500 feet. ITA’s crew also received a possible pilot deviation notification. There was also the December 2025 Houston encounter between Volaris El Salvador and a United Express regional jet. In that case, the Volaris crew read back a left turn correctly but turned right, toward the other departure. The United Express crew reported a collision avoidance advisory. I was reading about this incident on X and I found your blog by searching for this specific phrase: ““Fly heading of two seven zero immediately.”

As a non-native English speaker I found myself often struggling very much to understand air traffic controllers (in media, luckily I do not fly myself) because the radio communications are often unclear but also the phraseology is quite specific. What was this instruction supposed to mean? Doesn’t “fly heading of X” mean that pilot should turn X?

Again, not a pilot and not a native speaker, so excuse my ignorance please. Everyone in the thread was piling on the French pilot but a couple of people did bring this up, which made me search for an answer.

This keeps happening at LAX, different carriers, not great. It’s no longer merely a coincidence or ‘distracted pilots’… something isn’t right, and they need to address and resolve it.

Too many aircraft , too many flights , too little leeway . Reduce all flights by 75% , and stagger take-offs for one every 15 minutes .

I have recommended this for many years , yet they ludicrously keep adding more flights .

Seems like the American flight should have seen the Air France traffic if it was at 12 o’clock and at a slightly higher altitude. It was LAX so likely not IMC

Albert – no. Just no. Here are some crayons. Go color or something. Let the adults deal with this.

LAX has, on average, about 800 daily departures, or in excess of 290,000 takeoffs per year. Within the past five years, there have been FOUR highly-publicized incidents of a crew turning the wrong direction immediately after taking off in LAX. So it’s happening roughly 0.00137% of the time. Your idea is ludicrous to put it kindly.

As someone who’s flown into and out of LAX for decades, the problem almost always comes down to a pilot error. If you expect to depart runway 25R, and you set up the “box” (the FMS computer) for it, the route it “grabs” includes the early left turn used by 25R. Now, during taxi out, ATC gives you runway 24L for departure.

Every plane is a little different, but if you follow the correct, prescribed steps in the correct order needed – as you make the changes, the box will grab the associated route with 24L, and give you a course that’s nearly straight ahead instead – as it’s supposed to do. But if you short-cut the steps (just swap the runway, instead of reloading the departure procedure too) and it’s possible to get the 25R route with the 24L runway. That’s likely what happened here. The flight management computer will direct the southbound turn from the northern set of runways.

It is a mistake that becomes likely when a crew is 1) tired (long-haul flying is fatiguing by its very nature, even at the beginning of a flight), 2) tasked with a higher workload because they now must obtain new takeoff data because they got a different runway, and 3) faced increasing workload-management issues as they now received taxi instructions contrary to what they expected… as they are going to a new runway. Heads go “down” (one works on the box and the data, while the other makes sure to follow the correct taxi instructions), cross checking can get missed, and an error can be made.

The solution? No – it’s not to cut 75% of the system. That would make things LESS safe by reducing proficiency and experience. The industry would become less attractive, so fewer would aspire to it. The airline’s new pilot candidate aptitude would drop. Resources to improve safety would evaporate (which created, over the past few decades: GPWS, TCAS, CPDLC, vastly improved on-board weather radar, safety management programs, etc. etc. etc.). The solution is to continue to invest in pilot and ATC training. To insist on two pilots in the flight deck, and adequate training and staffing for ATC.

No aviation system can 100% eliminate all threats, errors, and mistakes (short of just grounding all flights, paving over all airports, and scrapping every plane in existence). What Albert doesn’t seem to realize is what we saw here was the system WORKING. When a mistake happens by one airline crew (the Air France flight) ATC was paying attention, and had the situational awareness to quickly address it. And the American crew was also trained, ready, and capable of quickly handling a non-routine instruction to get out of the way.

When mistakes happen – and they always will – the system needs to quickly catch it and provide a correction before things turn disastrous. That’s how it’s supposed to work, and that is exactly what it did.

PilotPaul – Lindbergh did OK whilst flying solo and without a FMS computer , because he did one take-off at a time . The problem here is too many take-offs and landings at one time .

This is not the elevated experience that LAX’s guests are accustomed to.

So you are equating a rickety, slow, experimental flight that took 33+ hours to complete – that same close to failure on several occasions during the flight (including the takeoff) – as the standard we should strive to duplicate?

PilotPaul – Lindbergh would not have allowed helicopters to cross flight paths at DCA . Lindbergh’s answer would be to reduce them and get a handle on it .

#6138. Air France A350 Nearly Collides Midair With American A321 After Wrong Turn At LAX

Journalist – Aaron is an aviation and travel journalist with 14 years of experience in the travel and tourism industry. His background spans airport operations, aviation infrastructure, and travel consulting, having worked with global organizations across New Zealand, Europe, and North America. Combining industry expertise with firsthand travel experience across more than 52 countries and five continents, Aaron covers airlines, airports, aviation policy, and the wider travel sector. He is based in Canterbury, New Zealand. His work has been published in Simple Flying and featured by MSN, SAM CHUI Aviation & Travel, EIN News, Pakistan Defence, and Climate Depot.

This article was updated on Monday, November 9, 2026, to include new details on the unauthorized turn and a similar 2025 incident. It was originally published on Sunday, November 8, 2026.

Two aircraft belonging to American Airlines and Air France came within 400 feet (121 meters) of vertical separation as both jets departed from Los Angeles International Airport (LAX). Quick actions by air traffic control and the pilots onboard averted a close call that could have had catastrophic consequences.

The two planes were departing from California's busiest airport in the early hours of Saturday morning. Air France Flight 28 was heading for Papeete (PPT), while American Flight 1660 was flying to Dallas/Fort Worth International Airport (DFW). The two jets — which collectively could have been carrying more than 500 passengers — came dangerously close to each other shortly after takeoff, before controllers intervened to prevent a potential collision.

The Air France Airbus A350-900, operating as AF28, had been cleared to take off from Los Angeles via the SUMMR2 procedure. SUMMR2, according to the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), is a set route that tells departing aircraft which direction to fly after takeoff. In this case, planes taking off from Runways 24L/R and 25L/R must initially climb straight ahead before following their assigned route.

At the same time, the American jet, destined for Texas, was told by air traffic control to stay at 2,000 feet, to allow the Air France widebody to turn and then head to FL270. However, an unauthorized turn by the Air France aircraft brought the two jets onto conflicting flight paths.

Simple Flying reached out to Air France for comment on the incident; however, an airline spokesperson could not immediately be reached.

According to TurbineTraveler on X, the Air France plane made an unauthorized turn left shortly after takeoff, rather than continuing straight as instructed. This placed the A350 directly in the trajectory of the departing American jet. This led the two planes to come within dangerous proximity of each other, known as a loss of separation event.

The controller quickly spotted the developing conflict and instructed both aircraft to turn away from each other. The controller then questioned the Air France crew about the deviation from its departure route. Both aircraft involved are detailed in the table below, with flight data captured from the Simple Flying Flight Tracker:

Both the American and Air France flights were then able to continue safely to their intended destinations with no reported injuries or harm to anyone on board. A similar incident occurred in Los Angeles in 2025, when an American and ITA Airways jet almost collided midair after a pilot deviation from the busy airport.

Two aircraft lost separation while climbing out of LAX.

So far, reports indicate that neither crew received a Traffic Collision Avoidance System (TCAS) resolution advisory, an automated cockpit warning that instructs pilots to climb or descend to avoid another aircraft. These alerts can prevent midair collisions when aircraft get too close, giving pilots immediate instructions to increase their separation.

Since the incident was first reported, outlets have published different figures for how close AF28 and AA1660 came to each other. According to The Aviation Herald, the A350 began turning left while climbing through 1,800 feet, despite its departure procedure calling for a straight climb to 5,000 feet.

The incident also bears striking similarities to an event involving ITA Airways in October 2025, when a Rome-bound Airbus A330-900 departing Runway 24L turned left toward an American A321 that had taken off from Runway 25R.

As one of the busiest airports in the US and the world, Los Angeles International Airport has carefully controlled departure routes to keep aircraft safely separated. The SUMMR2 procedure directs westbound departures out over the Pacific Ocean, helping keep them clear of other departing and arriving traffic.

SUMMR flights often transition to long-haul or coastal routes, including to destinations in Hawaii, Asia, and the north, like San Francisco. Instead of following this procedure, the Air France pilot made a sharp left turn shortly after departure, which intersected the path of the American jet that had departed from Runway 25R. Fortunately, the departure controller identified the conflict, and their swift actions resulted in the two planes being able to quickly change course and avoid a midair collision.

#6136. How To Combine World Of Hyatt Points Between Accounts For Free

The major hotel loyalty programs all have different policies when it comes to combining points between accounts belonging to different members. I’ve already covered the options and policies for Hilton Honors and Marriott Bonvoy, and in this post, I’d like to take a look at the policy of World of Hyatt.

The good news is that World of Hyatt recently introduced a new way to transfer points to others for free, and I’d argue the program now has among the most generous policies in the industry. Long story short, you can transfer or receive up to 525,000 points per year, and this can all be done online, and at no cost. In this post, I’d like to look more closely at the mechanics of Hyatt points transfers.

World of Hyatt offers a generous feature to allow members to transfer points to others at no cost. Let’s first cover the basic rules for Hyatt points transfers:

It’s worth noting that this system is much better than it used to be. Back in the day combining Hyatt points required completing a form and took days, and you could only combine points in order to have sufficient points for a specific redemption. That policy no longer applies.

The process of transferring World of Hyatt points between members online is straightforward. To start, you can either follow this link, or go to your account overview page, and go to the section that reads “Gift your points more seamlessly.”

On the next page, you’ll want to go to the “Gift points or eligible awards” section, and then click “Gift your points.”

There you’ll first want to select how many points you want to transfer, using the slider.

Then on the next page, you’ll need to enter the account information for the account you want to move points to.

Then you’ll just need to confirm the details, and that’s it! Regarding transfer times, reports suggest transfers take anywhere from a few minutes to several days. It does seem like the more points you transfer, the more likely that it takes days for the transfer to go through. So if you are moving a large chunk of points, don’t be surprised if it takes some time.

What are the benefits to being able to combine points between World of Hyatt accounts? On the most basic level, it allows you to combine points so you have enough for an award stay. In other words, if you have two accounts with 15,000 points each, you can combine the points so you have enough for a one night stay at a hotel costing 30,000 points.

Furthermore, if you’re traveling as multiple people and one person has elite status, there’s value to booking the stay out of their account, so that you could take advantage of World of Hyatt Globalist or World of Hyatt Explorist benefits, for example.

However, thanks to the Guest of Honor program, it’s actually pretty easy to give elite perks to friends and family nowadays. For that matter, even Suite Upgrade Awards and Club Access Awards are transferable nowadays.

Lastly, combining points is also considered “activity” for the purposes of keeping your account alive, so it would reset the expiration of points.

World of Hyatt has a great system for letting members combine and share points. World of Hyatt members can transfer up to 525,000 points per year to other members, with limited restrictions. This is possible online, and typically points transfers happen pretty quickly.

There’s lots of value to this, and I’d say Hyatt’s policy is comparable to Hilton Honors for being the best in the industry.

If you’ve ever combined World of Hyatt points, what was your experience like?

Membership is free and takes no more information than commenting as a guest. Earn status points for good contributions, and see fewer ads as your status grows.

Your feedback is important in helping us keep our community safe.

The comments on this page have not been provided, reviewed, approved or otherwise endorsed by any advertiser, and it is not an advertiser's responsibility to ensure posts and/or questions are answered.

These guides are extremely helpful, Ben. It’s as if these programs try to hide the ways to do this; thankfully, you’re got us covered. Seriously, to the programs that don’t allow free transfers between members, that’s so lame. We really should have that as a basic consumer protection by now… *sigh*

#6133. Finnair’s Cheap Avios Sale Offers A Shortcut To Status On American Flights And Access To Flagship Lounges

Finnair is selling 200,000 Avios for $2,170, and throwing in 20,000 points towards elite status. Those Avios can buy business class awards on Finnair, or move over to British Airways and Qatar Airways. And the status points can help you get into American Airlines Flagship lounges even when you’re flying domestic coach. The purchase alone gets you Finnair Silver, which is oneworld Ruby, and I don’t see much value in chasing Ruby. You get some airport priority on American and Alaska and a free checked bag. Finnair Gold, which is oneworld Sapphire, comes with lounge access including business class Flagship lounge access. The latest Frequent Miler on the Air episode walks through the sale and ways to leverage it. One Mile at a Time covered the offer when it launched. I’ve written about buying Finnair points to earn oneworld status since November 2020, and covered another version in December 2021. Those offers could get you all the way to Sapphire or Emerald without flying. This one is less generous for status, but the redeemable points are much more useful now that Finnair uses Avios than they were back then. What The Avios Cost Now The sale runs through November 16, 2026, ending at 4:59 p.m. Eastern. You need to have joined Finnair Plus before October 30 and have at least 50 Avios in your account. The purchase allowance has been reset for this offer: you can buy up to 200,000 even if you already hit the normal annual limit. The discount reaches 50% at 85,000 Avios. The best dollar pricing is available on purchases of 100,000 or more: 1.085 cents per Avios, before card rewards or shopping portal earnings. The purchase also generates tier points equal to 10% of the Avios bought. The podcast described paying in Japanese yen for about 1.06 cents apiece, then earning 3 points per dollar on an Atmos Rewards Summit card’s foreign purchases category. That yen price is no longer available and dollars are now the better deal. Purchases are processed by Points.com, not as airline tickets. Use a card with a strong return on otherwise unbonused spending. Finnair’s milestone rewards add another layer of benefits. A Basic member crossing 12,000 tier points receives 3,000 extra Avios. Starting at zero, and assuming that milestone hasn’t already been earned: Purchase Dollar Cost Avios Including Milestone Tier Points 120,000 Avios $1,302 123,000 12,000 150,000 Avios $1,627.50 153,000 15,000 200,000 Avios $2,170 203,000 20,000 The 120,000-point purchase works out to about 1.059 cents per Avios after the milestone. That’s slightly cheaper per point than buying the maximum. Existing Gold members don’t receive this Basic-tier milestone (Finnair only awards milestones within your own tier). Frequent Miler also flagged Rove at 1 mile per dollar and Extrabux at 1.6%–2% cash back as potential shopping portal optins to start with when buying the points. $1,302 would earn 1,302 Rove miles, which are also transferable to Finnair. Ruby Isn’t The Status I’d Spend Money Chasing Silver requires 15,000 tier points (not 20,000 as some discussions suggest, which is actually a separate milestone awarding two Finnair lounge passes). Buying 150,000 Avios already earns Silver from zero. Ruby gets you business class check-in and some seating and waitlist benefits. On American, it also means a free first checked bag and Group 4 boarding. Finnair Gold gives you oneworld business class lounge access, along with additional baggage and priority services. And because the status comes from Finnair rather than American or Alaska, American permits Flagship lounge access on eligible domestic trips as well. You can bring one guest. It doesn’t include Flagship Dining. You also get Admirals Club access and Alaska Lounge access when flying either airline. Gold also comes with four Finnair upgrade benefits covering one short-haul economy-to-business upgrade each or U.S.–Helsinki would use all four, requiring upgrade availability. You can also exchange all four for a two-for-one Finnair Classic economy or premium economy award. How To Get From This Sale To Sapphire Finnair Gold requires 45,000 tier points. Starting from zero, buying the maximum gives you 20,000. You can then exchange 22,500 Avios for 7,500 tier points. That leaves you with 27,500 tier points, 17,500 short of Gold, and 180,500 redeemable Avios if you received the Basic milestone. Finnair allows one exchange per personal tracking period, at three Avios per tier point, with a 500-tier-point minimum and a €10 online fee. The ceiling depends on your status when you exchange: 7,500 tier points for Basic or Silver, 22,500 for Gold, and 40,000 for Platinum or Platinum Lumo. An existing Gold member has a much easier renewal calculation. Buying 200,000 Avios generates 20,000 tier points, and converting 67,500 Avios adds 22,500. That’s 42,500 towards the 45,000 needed, leaving just 2,500 to earn if you started the period at zero. You’d retain 132,500 purchased Avios. For someone starting without status, American flights can fill the 17,500-point gap. Finnair’s earning chart for business class, including domestic flights with Finnair Silver status: J, C and D earn 250% of distance before the Silver bonus, or 275% with it. You’d need about 6,364 flown miles to generate 17,500 tier points. R and I earn 150%, or 165% with the Silver bonus. You’d need about 10,607 flown miles. Check your account’s personal tracking period before doing any of this. It isn’t the calendar year, and buying points or reaching Silver doesn’t restart it. Purchase, conversion and remaining flight credit need to fall in the same period. Once you reach Gold, the status lasts for the rest of that period plus the following 12 months. You Can Use Credit Card Points For The Final Top-Up You don’t have to buy Avios to use the conversion feature. If you’re 3,000 tier points short of Gold, you can transfer in 9,000 Avios and exchange them, paying the €10 online fee. Capital One transfers directly to Finnair at 1:1. Or transfer a bank currency into British Airways, then move those Avios into Finnair. Qatar Avios can go through British Airways to reach Finnair, too. Finnair’s current linking rules require an account at least 30 days old, matching names and email addresses, and two-factor authentication. That’s important even for getting the 50 Avios needed for the sale since an account opened shortly before the October 30 cutoff may qualify for the promotion but still be too new for an Avios-program transfer. The Avios You’re Buying Are Valuable, Too I covered Finnair’s improved award opportunities in May 2024. You can redeem through Finnair or move Avios 1:1, without a transfer fee, to British Airways and onward to Qatar or other Avios programs as well. You can redeem through Finnair or move Avios 1:1, without a transfer fee, to British Airways and onward to Qatar or other Avios programs as well. Silver requires 15,000 tier points (not 20,000 as some discussions suggest, which is actually a separate milestone awarding two Finnair lounge passes). Buying 150,000 Avios already earns Silver from zero.

Ruby gets you business class check-in and some seating and waitlist benefits. On American, it also means a free first checked bag and Group 4 boarding.

Finnair Gold gives you oneworld business class lounge access, along with additional baggage and priority services. And because the status comes from Finnair rather than American or Alaska, American permits Flagship lounge access on eligible domestic trips as well. You can bring one guest. It doesn’t include Flagship Dining.

You also get Admirals Club access and Alaska Lounge access when flying either airline.

Gold also comes with four Finnair upgrade benefits covering one short-haul economy-to-business upgrade each or U.S.–Helsinki would use all four, requiring upgrade availability. You can also exchange all four for a two-for-one Finnair Classic economy or premium economy award.

Finnair Gold requires 45,000 tier points. Starting from zero, buying the maximum gives you 20,000. You can then exchange 22,500 Avios for 7,500 tier points. That leaves you with 27,500 tier points, 17,500 short of Gold, and 180,500 redeemable Avios if you received the Basic milestone. Finnair allows one exchange per personal tracking period, at three Avios per tier point, with a 500-tier-point minimum and a €10 online fee. The ceiling depends on your status when you exchange: 7,500 tier points for Basic or Silver, 22,500 for Gold, and 40,000 for Platinum or Platinum Lumo. An existing Gold member has a much easier renewal calculation. Buying 200,000 Avios generates 20,000 tier points, and converting 67,500 Avios adds 22,500. That’s 42,500 towards the 45,000 needed, leaving just 2,500 to earn if you started the period at zero. You’d retain 132,500 purchased Avios. For someone starting without status, American flights can fill the 17,500-point gap. Finnair’s earning chart for business class, including domestic flights with Finnair Silver status: J, C and D earn 250% of distance before the Silver bonus, or 275% with it. You’d need about 6,364 flown miles to generate 17,500 tier points. R and I earn 150%, or 165% with the Silver bonus. You’d need about 10,607 flown miles. Check your account’s personal tracking period before doing any of this. It isn’t the calendar year, and buying points or reaching Silver doesn’t restart it. Purchase, conversion and remaining flight credit need to fall in the same period. Once you reach Gold, the status lasts for the rest of that period plus the following 12 months. You Can Use Credit Card Points For The Final Top-Up You don’t have to buy Avios to use the conversion feature. If you’re 3,000 tier points short of Gold, you can transfer in 9,000 Avios and exchange them, paying the €10 online fee. Capital One transfers directly to Finnair at 1:1. Or transfer a bank currency into British Airways, then move those Avios into Finnair. Qatar Avios can go through British Airways to reach Finnair, too. Finnair’s current linking rules require an account at least 30 days old, matching names and email addresses, and two-factor authentication. That’s important even for getting the 50 Avios needed for the sale since an account opened shortly before the October 30 cutoff may qualify for the promotion but still be too new for an Avios-program transfer. You can redeem through Finnair or move Avios 1:1, without a transfer fee, to British Airways and onward to Qatar or other Avios programs as well. #6132. Which Airlines Fly To The Most Destinations? Some May Surprise You

Recently, I wrote a post about the airlines that fly to the most countries. Turkish Airlines wins that title by a long shot, and has a 30+ country lead over the second most “global” airline.

In this post, I want to address a different but related topic — which airlines serve the most destinations? As you’d expect, this is a very different list. That’s because serving a lot of countries is much easier if you’re an airline that has a lot of service in Europe and Africa, given the number of countries there that are in close proximity. It’s one of the reason that US airlines don’t score that well when it comes to absolute number of countries served, despite otherwise being among the biggest carriers in the world.

However, the list of total number of destinations served is a different story…

I don’t think anyone will be surprised by the three airlines that serve the most destinations. As it currently stands:

This makes sense. In terms of fleets, the “big three” US carriers are among the biggest in the world. A majority of their networks are domestic, which is why the airlines don’t rank that high when it comes to total number of countries served, but they do great when it comes to the total number of destinations served. Note that the number of destinations also includes flights operated by their regional subsidiaries.

I don’t think the order above will surprise anyone. United is of course the most global US airline, and has a very impressive route network, including with ultra long haul flights. Meanwhile American is a massive domestic airline, and has a strong network in Latin America and the Caribbean, which is why it doesn’t appear that far behind United in terms of international destinations. And Delta, ummm, gets a revenue premium.

Just in the interest of being thorough, I’m sure some people are curious how many destinations Southwest serves, since it’s an absolutely massive airline in the United States, though doesn’t operate long haul flights. That number is less impressive — it’s a total of 120 destinations, including 104 domestic destinations and 16 international destinations. That’s because the airline is more about depth of service than breadth of service, and doesn’t have a regional subsidiary.

After US carriers, which airlines otherwise top the list of most destinations served? Most people wouldn’t be surprised to learn that Turkish takes that spot, serving 269 destinations, including 46 domestic destinations and 223 international destinations.

What about after that? Here are the next eight airlines (I think this is where some of the airlines may surprise people):

It’s interesting just how different the airlines on the list are. You have the “big three” Chinese carriers, the “big three” European carriers, and then you have Ryanair and Air Canada.

When you put it all together, below is the chart with the 12 airlines serving the most total destinations.

In the interest of being thorough, for those curious about Gulf carriers, Qatar Airways is in first place among them, serving 175 destinations, so it doesn’t quite make the list. Meanwhile Ethiopian Airlines, as Africa’s most global airline, serves 163 destinations

While Turkish Airlines flies to the most countries of any airline in the world, it doesn’t serve the most destinations. Instead that title goes to United, with the “big three” US carriers taking the three top spots. Then Turkish is in fourth place, and is followed by the “big three” Chinese carriers, the “big three” European carriers, and then also Ryanair and Air Canada.

Are you surprised by any of the airlines serving the most destinations?

#6130. American Airlines Updates Vouchers For Stranded Passengers—But Tells Employees There May Be Fewer Hotel Choices

American Airlines is updating how stranded passengers get hotel rooms, meal credits and rides during flight disruptions. An internal November memo I reviewed lays out automatic offers for eligible overnight delays and a new way for agents to arrange Uber rides without making passengers download the app. It also warns that employees may see fewer hotels to choose from. Getting passengers out of the customer service line and into a room sooner is great for getting sleep. On a recent American Airlines flight from New York to Austin that was cancelled after a long delay I didn’t even bother getting into the long line at the gate for a room voucher, I just booked something myself nad went on my way. What American Is Changing The update covers American’s Hotel, Meal and Transportation system, which employees call HMT. October 26: standalone meal credits. Agents can issue food and beverage credits for individual reservations affected by qualifying delays, cancellations and missed connections. The system uses flight information to evaluate eligibility and tells agents what qualifies. October 27: automatic offers for eligible overnight delays. The system sends hotel offers and applicable food and beverage credits when its eligibility and automation criteria are met, reducing the need for an employee to initiate the offer. Planned Uber Central rollout. At participating airports, authorized agents would arrange a ride on the customer’s behalf through the same system. The passenger receives a text message or WhatsApp link to start the ride, without downloading Uber. This should now be available but I haven’t seen passenger reports of the broadly available rollout yet (though customers reported it in limited release previously). Hotel inventory changes, date undetermined. American is changing the hotel inventory feed and selection process. Employees are told they may see fewer hotel choices. Automatic Vouchers Already Exist American has been working on this for years. I covered the electronic hotel and meal system in 2019, when agents still had to qualify customers and trigger offers. American was already describing automatic hotel, meal and transportation vouchers in 2025. This spring, they added meal issuance for an entire flight at once. In June, automatic meal vouchers expanded beyond elite members to all AAdvantage members. American’s January app changes already brought disruption assistance together: Their published customer service plan promises, upon request, an approved hotel for an overnight disruption they cause away from your city of residence, transportation there and back, and a food and beverage credit after a qualifying delay of at least three hours. The standard meal voucher I’ve been covering is $12. American recently renamed it a “food/beverage credit” because calling it a meal voucher led passengers to expect it to pay for a meal. How The Uber Change Works American already offers Uber vouchers. The change lets an agent arrange the ride for the passenger. Uber Central supports rides paid for by the business, with trip details sent to the customer. However, American’s instructions still put the hotel shuttle first, followed by an Uber voucher. Uber Central is for exceptions when those options don’t meet the customer’s needs. One passenger reported being at Washington National when agents refused Uber vouchers because a hotel had a shuttle even though it wasn’t running at 1 a.m. Fewer Hotel Choices Isn’t Great The memo’s most concerning sentence is: Frontline teams may see fewer hotel choices displayed than they are accustomed to seeing. Being able to choose a hotel matters. I’ve covered passenger complaints about unsuitable rooms and missing shuttles. Here’s a passenger who said the hotel floor was so dirty they spread sheets over it. If American can’t provide an approved hotel voucher, its customer service plan promises reimbursement of reasonable hotel costs. Its conditions of carriage also say reimbursement isn’t guaranteed when you book directly without written authorization. Credit card trip protections may reimburse required hotel overnights as well. Topics on this pageAmerican AirlinesUberAAdvantageNew YorkWhatsApp+3 more More From View from the Wing

On a recent trip through Chicago O’Hare International Airport (ORD), I missed my connecting flight to the East Coast. Unless American Airlines (AA) somehow anticipated that my connecting flight would depart more than two hours late, the airline knew well in advance of my arrival at ORD, that I was likely to be stranded at ORD.

To make matters worse, my arrival at ORD was already more than two hours behind schedule because AA had knowingly oversold my original flight and apparently had to beg, borrow, and steal to get approximately 20 passengers off the flight so that it could depart. Given these circumstances, I would have expected AA to proactively make arrangements for displaced passengers, including securing hotel accommodations for those who would inevitably miss their connections.

Instead, when I approached the AA agents at ORD to request a hotel room, they appeared genuinely surprised by my request. Eventually, an agent provided me with a hotel voucher, round-trip taxi vouchers for transportation between the airport and a Courtyard by Marriott approximately 20 minutes away, and a nominal credit for food and beverages.

I find it difficult to believe that the deplorable establishment to which AA sent me was actually operating under the Courtyard by Marriott name. The hotel with which AA apparently has a contractual arrangement to accommodate stranded passengers was filthy, disgusting, and wholly unacceptable. It resembled a seedy, hourly-rate establishment far more than a Marriott-branded hotel. Frankly, it was a place I wouldn’t send my dog. I cannot imagine what AA was thinking when it selected this property to accommodate its passengers.

And the experience didn’t end there. Not a single taxi in the ORD taxi queue would accept AA’s taxi voucher. The same thing happened when I attempted to return to the airport. I would expect American Airlines to treat a dog better than it treated me. Perhaps, however, in AA’s eyes, paying passengers have been relegated to little more than a nuisance.

That is certainly how I was made to feel.

As High As 300,000 points. Find Out Your Offer.

As High As 175,000 points. Find Out Your Offer.

You don't have to be a Marriott Bonvoy loyalist to find ongoing value in the (see rates and fees).

The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless stands out in the Marriott card suite thanks to its solid lineup of perks, including an annual free night award (certain hotels have resort fees) and elite night credits, for a relatively low annual fee.

Whether you are a frequent Marriott guest or want a few extra perks the next time you stay with the brand, the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless makes sense for a wide range of travelers. Card rating*: ⭐⭐⭐⭐

*Card rating is based on the opinion of TPG's editors and is not influenced by the card issuer.

The is a cobranded card between Marriott Bonvoy and Chase. The card earns Marriott Bonvoy points, which can be used to book free nights at more than 10,000 properties worldwide.

The best way to redeem Marriott points is for free nights at Marriott hotels and resorts. However, you can also transfer your points to airline partners.

Marriott Bonvoy Boundless provides a standout suite of perks, including an annual free night award and automatic Silver Elite status, for a $95 annual fee.

I find it especially impressive that a mid-tier hotel card with a modest annual fee offers such lucrative perks, especially the annual free night award. Certain hotels have resort fees.

Here's a breakdown of the perks included with the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless:

You don't have to go all in on Marriott to get a lot out of having this $95-annual-fee card in your wallet, and that's what makes the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless worth considering.

Related: Marriott Bonvoy elite status 'soft landing' policy: How to requalify for status

The packs a punch for its reasonable annual fee. Here's what cardholders can expect.

Given TPG's November 2026 valuation of Marriott points at 0.75 cents apiece, the 35,000-point certificate is worth $263. This is nearly three times the card's $95 annual fee and is a fantastic benefit, especially since you don't have to spend on the card to earn the certificate.

While the Silver Elite status on the card is the first of Marriott's elite status tiers, it does offer a few useful benefits, such as a 10% points bonus on paid stays and priority late checkout.

If you put at least $35,000 of spending on the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless in a calendar year, you'll earn Gold Elite status. This comes with more perks, such as a 25% points boost and enhanced room upgrade (when available).

For most cardholders, it’s hard to justify putting $35,000 in purchases on the card solely to earn Gold Elite status.

If Gold Elite status is your goal, you may be better off combining the card's 15 complimentary elite night credits with 10 paid nights; this totals 25 elite nights needed for Gold Elite status.

If you're eligible for a business card, you can also pair the 15 elite night credits given by the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless with 15 elite night credits provided by the . These 30 total elite night credits leave you with just 20 nights to earn Platinum Elite.

You can also reach a higher elite status by earning one elite night credit for every $5,000 spent on purchases with the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless.

Related: How to choose a no-foreign-transaction-fee credit card

Given TPG's relatively low valuation of Marriott points, I only recommend paying for Marriott stays with the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless. There are other cards on the market that earn more valuable rewards on dining, gas and groceries.

The best way to redeem your Marriott points is to book free nights at one of the brand's hotels.

Since Marriott uses dynamic award pricing (meaning the number of points needed fluctuates based on demand and availability), you may have to take extra time and effort to strategize for maximum value.

Marriott has an award calendar search function that can help narrow down the best deal for your points. For example, a night at the Moxy NYC Lower East Side in January 2027 could cost as few as 57,000 points per night or as many as 81,000 points per night, depending on when you book.

While we value Marriott points at 0.75 cents apiece, there are ways to get better value.

For instance, TPG lead writer for loyalty programs Katie Genter previously redeemed 112,000 points for a five-night stay at the Courtyard by Marriott Toronto Vaughan for a music festival. Compared against a cash rate of $1,464, she got an impressive 1.31 cents per point from this redemption.

Also, keep in mind that Marriott offers a fifth-night-free benefit. When you book at least five consecutive nights on points, you'll get the night that's worth the lowest number of points for free. This can help you stretch your points for longer trips.

Marriott points are also transferable to nearly 40 airline partners, most at a 3:1 ratio. These include some hard-to-earn currencies, such as Air China PhoenixMiles and Frontier Airlines.

However, unless you have a specific airline redemption in mind and need to top off your balance, transferring is unlikely to be the best use of your points.

Related: Can you mix hotel points and free night certificates for a fourth or fifth night free?

The won't be the perfect fit for everyone. Here are some shortfalls to consider:

The is a premium sibling to the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless. It charges a much higher $650 annual fee (see rates and fees) but provides more benefits for Marriott loyalists.

These perks include higher Platinum Elite status, 25 elite night credits each calendar year toward status and an annual free night award valued at 85,000 points. (Certain hotels have resort fees.)

To learn more, read our showdown of the Bonvoy Boundless versus the Bonvoy Brilliant.

Related: 3 reasons why the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless is worth the $95 annual fee

Currently, new cardholders can earn three free night awards* after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Additionally, they can receive up to $100 in statement credits (up to $50 biannually) after spending $500 on eligible airline purchases (through June 30, 2027).

*Nights are valued at up to 50,000 points each; certain hotels have resort fees.

If you max out the free night awards and earn the statement credits for airline purchases, this bonus is worth up to $1,225 per TPG's valuations.

The current offer delivers decent value for new cardholders. That said, we've seen stronger welcome offers on the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless in the past.

We generally recommend applying when the welcome offer includes at least 150,000 bonus points or at least four free night awards (each valued at up to 50,000 points).

Related: The best credit card welcome bonuses available now

The has multiple competitors. Here are a few to consider:

For additional options, see our list of the best hotel credit cards.

Related: Which credit card should you use for Marriott stays?

I find the to be an excellent choice for a wide range of travelers, from Marriott loyalists who don't want to pay a high annual fee to those who occasionally stay at the brand's hotels and resorts.

This is because you get solid ongoing value from the annual free night award without paying a high annual fee.

Of course, if you're a fierce Marriott loyalist chasing status, a more premium card may be a better choice. And, if you want an option that earns higher-value rewards at a better rate on everyday purchases, you may want to look at a general travel card that earns transferable rewards.

Overall, however, the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless certainly provides enough ongoing value in exchange for its modest $95 annual fee, making it worth keeping year after year.

I have the card. I’m keeping it because it allows you to have the same purchases earn credit towards status for two people. For instance,

$125,000 in eligible spending on an employee card can produce 125,000 Loyalty Points for the employee and another 125,000 Loyalty Points for the primary cardmember. That’s enough for both to earn Platinum Pro status. On an American Airlines personal card, only one person would earn this status. It’s leverage no other airline’s card offers. Put spending on an employee card, and both that individual and the primary cardholder earns status credit from the same spending. American lists this as valid through December 31, 2028 but that doesn’t mean it won’t be extended. American’s business card earns redeemable miles that go into the company’s AAdvantage Business account, which are also transferable to individual AAdvantage accounts and you can choose where they go later. Those thresholds are triggered by Loyalty Points earned across your AAdvantage account, and doesn’t require spending a single dollar on the Executive card itself. I’m a primary Citi Executive card holder. If I get one for my wife, then $105,000 on her business employee card would produce 105,000 Loyalty Points for each of us plus 20,000 in Executive card bonuses apiece. $105,000 spend becomes enough for two Platinum Pro and oneworld emerald statuses (without loyalty points from any other source, including Citi Globe’s ‘flight streak’ bonus). The card earns: 3 miles per dollar on eligible bookings through AAdvantage Hotels and AAdvantage Cars. 2 miles per dollar in one chosen category: U.S. shipping, office supply stores, or U.S. advertising. And it offers a $100 inflight credit which covers food, beverages and Wi-Fi. Spend $30,000 during your cardmembership year and renew, and you can earn a certificate for a companion’s eligible domestic Main Cabin roundtrip for $99 plus taxes and fees. The card also receives first checked bag free on eligible domestic itineraries and preferred boarding for the primary cardmember and up to four companions on the same reservation, 10% off eligible American Airlines Vacations packages, and no foreign transaction fees. #6124. Trans Thai Women Stole Tourist’s $600,000 Watch Over $60 Dispute—They ‘Thought It Was Fake’

A Chinese tourist says two women took his diamond-covered Patek Philippe and passport from his Pattaya hotel room. He valued the watch at roughly $600,000. When they demanded about $600 to return his belongings, he paid but only got his passport back. Police recovered the watch and arrested two suspects early Sunday morning. The suspects told police they were owed 2,000 baht (~ $60) and thought the watch was fake. The tourist reported the theft November 7 from room 309 at the Z8 Hotel. He said two transgender women took the watch and passport, then demanded 20,000 baht to return them. After collecting the cash, they returned the passport and left with the watch. The silver-colored, diamond-set Patek Philippe PP5719G can actually list at $725,000. The two suspects were arrested early in the morning of November 8. They claimed they’d just taken the watch figuring it was worth what they were owed (what they were owed for you can leave to your imagination). I’ve written about a guest who arrived at a Marriott wearing a $24,000 Rolex but hadn’t booked the night of his arrival. He fell asleep in the lobby waiting for a room, and someone took it right off his wrist. And in the stranger hotel watch recovery, two Rolexes taken from guests at Encore Las Vegas were concealed inside the women who stole them. A reader’s response to that story evokes Pulp Fiction: I don’t think I would ever wear the watch again. There is not enough disinfectant in the world. Now I can’t get images of the thieves looking just like Christopher Walken out of my mind. Y’all be careful on your travels out there! #6123. Can You Redeem Hotel Points For Others? Yes, You Just Have To Know How

One of the nice things about miles & points is being able to share the gift of travel with friends and family. Now, ideally we’d always be able to go along on those journeys, but there are some situations where that’s not practical, for obvious reasons.

Many people wonder if it’s possible to share their points with others, so they can enjoy a hotel stay. This is a great question, so I’d like to take a look at the policy of each individual program. While hotel loyalty programs in some ways offer more flexibility than airline loyalty programs, this isn’t necessarily one of those areas, as you sometimes have to jump through some hoops. For what it’s worth, in a separate post, I’ve addressed whether you can redeem airline miles for others.

All major hotel loyalty programs have some sort of policy for allowing you to redeem your points for others. In some cases you can directly make a reservation for others, while in other cases you need to transfer your points to another member (at no cost).

Let’s break this down by program. Before we start, let me emphasize a couple of important points:

With that out of the way, let’s get into it…

Accor Live Limitless (ALL) is the one hotel loyalty program that doesn’t let you redeem points for others. However, that’s not necessarily a huge loss. Keep in mind that Accor’s program is revenue based, and every 1,000 Accor points gets you €20 toward a hotel stay folio. You can use this for your own rooms or the rooms of those traveling with you, but you can’t just gift them to a third party.

Choice Privileges allows members to redeem points for reward nights for immediate family members, including a spouse, partner, children parents, in-laws, brothers, and sisters.

You can book a reward night for someone else in one of two ways. If you book through your online profile, be sure to include the name of the guest who will be staying in the room in the “Special Request” field. Alternatively, if booking by phone, ask the reservations agent to include the name of the guest in the notes field of the reservation.

Global Hotel Alliance’s GHA Discovery program is one that I’ve become increasingly intrigued by in recent times, given that it’s associated with dozens of independent hotel groups. GHA Discovery doesn’t have points, but instead, has D$, or Discovery Dollars, as they’re called. Each D$ gets you a dollar off an eligible hotel stay.

What’s cool is that you can actually transfer your D$ to others. A transfer can be initiated through the GHA Discovery app, and you just have to enter the recipient’s membership number and last name. You can begin sharing D$ if you’ve been a member of the program for at least 90 days, and you can perform or receive up to two transfers daily, with a minimum of D$100 and a maximum of D$500 per transaction.

The best way to book a Hilton Honors stay for someone else is to simply transfer points to their Hilton Honors account. Hilton has a free points sharing feature, whereby you can transfer points to another Hilton Honors member. You can transfer no more than 500,000 points to another member, and can receive no more than two million points per calendar year from others. That’s the easiest and most foolproof way to go about this.

One alternative is that you could call Hilton Honors to make a reservation, and explain you want to redeem your points for others. They might be able to book the reservation so that the second guest is listed on the reservation, and it’s documented that this is a gift. However, this might not be quite as seamless as just transferring your points to someone else.

One other option people use is that they’ll make a booking in their own name, and then in the “Add guest names” field on the payment page on Hilton’s website or app, they’ll add the name of the guest in the “Additional guests” field. I’ll talk more about this below — while this might work, it’s not really the official method you should use.

IHG One Rewards’ official policy is that you can book a reward night (either with points or free night awards) for someone else by making a booking via IHG’s website, and then adding an additional name to the reservation. In other words, you’re basically just making a reservation for yourself, with a second guest listed.

There’s also a comments section when making an IHG booking, so I’d recommend writing in that section about your intention to gift an award to someone else.

Marriott Bonvoy allows you to redeem your points directly for others, with some restrictions:

Another option is that Marriott Bonvoy lets you combine points between accounts. You can transfer up to 100,000 points per calendar year, and you can receive up to 500,000 points per calendar year. That’s the biggest restriction, as 100,000 points won’t get you very far, at least for an extended luxury hotel stay. Still, this is a feature I find to be useful.

With World of Hyatt there are a couple of practical ways to redeem points for others. The first is that World of Hyatt lets you outright redeem points or free night certificates for others. This can simply be done by contacting World of Hyatt customer service by phone, and they can process this request, or alternatively, you can transfer reward certificates to someone else’s World of Hyatt account.

If you have World of Hyatt Globalist status, keep in mind that you can also earn Guest of Honor certificates. These allow you to essentially share your Globalist perks with a friend or family member, regardless of whether or not they’re traveling with you. You can apply this either to a stay booked with cash or points, and you can either book the Guest of Honor award out of your account, or you can transfer the Guest of Honor certificate to someone else.

You even get one elite night credit in your own account for each certificate that’s gifted to someone else, after it’s redeemed. This is one of my favorite loyalty perks out there, and it’s a great way to share hotel elite status perks with others.

The other thing to keep in mind is that Hyatt lets you combine points with anyone else at no cost, and this can be done online, through the Hyatt website or app. The person doesn’t have to be related to you, and doesn’t have to live at the same address as you.

The only limitations are that you can transfer up to 525,000 points per year, and can make no more than six points transfers per calendar year. This is probably the easiest option, since the person can just directly redeem out of their own account.

Wyndham Rewards allows members to redeem points for reward nights for friends and family, with no limitations.

This is super straightforward. You can book a stay using points in someone else’s name either directly through the Wyndham Rewards website, or by calling Wyndham Rewards member services. There are no hoops to jump through.

People will often point out “oh, the best way to make a hotel reservation for someone else is to just book it for yourself, and then add the actual guest as the second person on the reservation.” As people view it, the upside is that it lets you earn points, and also share elite perks with others. However, unless explicitly noted above, this isn’t how it’s supposed to work.

It goes without saying that technically you’re only supposed to be able to earn points and take advantage of elite perks if you are actually staying, as the elite member. That’s not to say that this method won’t work sometimes. However, there are some things to keep in mind:

I play by the rules, but there are also plenty of situations where Ford arrives at a hotel before I do (I often take a different and more circuitous routing to get places), and he almost never has issues checking in, and I never even have to go to the front desk.

I’m not making a judgment call here one way or another, but I would only even remotely consider doing this if you and the actual guest both know what you’re doing.

Just about all major hotel loyalty programs let you redeem points for others, though the process varies by program. In some cases you can transfer your points to others, while in other cases you can just redeem a reward for others.

Regardless of which method you choose, just keep in mind that you can’t barter hotel points, and also that your elite perks generally won’t transfer over to others (with the exception of World of Hyatt’s Guest of Honor feature).

If you’ve redeemed hotel points for others, what was your experience like?

#6121. Free GHA Titanium Hotel Status For Bank Of America’s $100,000 Rewards Tier

If you have $100,000 in qualifying Bank of America and Merrill balances, check your banking rewards before paying for hotel elite status. There’s a reported benefit tucked inside the program that gets you GHA Discovery Titanium, with no hotel stay required. On the November 6 Frequent Miler on the Air episode, Greg Davis-Kean said he used this himself. His status upgrade was instant and runs through December 31, 2027. I’ve called GHA my second favorite hotel loyalty program, after Hyatt. I’ve received real benefits at hotels I actually wanted to stay in. Where To Find The Bank Of America Offer Greg reports that it works for Preferred Honors and Premier members, as a one-time match. That’s based on banking relationship tier rather than specific card product. Bank of America publishes the requirements for access to its lifestyle benefits: Preferred Honors requires an eligible checking account and a combined three-month average daily balance of at least $100,000 in qualifying Bank of America deposits and/or Merrill investment accounts. Premier generally starts at $1 million. Bank of America Private Bank clients can qualify for Premier regardless of balances. Enrolled members can find lifestyle benefits under the Rewards tab in online banking or MyMerrill, or through the lifestyle benefits tile in BofA Rewards. Look in the travel offers for GHA Discovery and follow the specific activation link. The $100,000 doesn’t have to be cash in a checking account, it includes investments at Merrill count. The Value Of GHA Titanium Status GHA Discovery is the loyalty program for roughly 1,000 hotels across about 60 brands, including Kempinski, Anantara, Capella, Pan Pacific, NH and Lore Group. It’s a way for smaller hotel groups to offer recognition and rewards across a much larger collection. I covered the program’s relaunch in December 2021, when it added Discovery Dollars (essentially, points-earning, it had been primarily a recognition program before that) and made status easier to earn. Titanium is the highest published tier. Normally, Titanium takes 30 eligible nights, $15,000 in eligible spending, or stays at three qualifying brands in a calendar year. The main Titanium benefits are: A two-category room upgrade, subject to availability, and that can be a suite. 11 a.m. early check-in and 4 p.m. late checkout, both subject to availability. Request early check-in at least two days ahead. A welcome amenity. 7% back in Discovery Dollars on eligible spending. Each dollar is worth one U.S. dollar towards eligible hotel charges, and regularly earned Titanium dollars expire after 24 months. There’s also breakfast for two at participating brands on direct bookings. This has expanded since I covered the benefit’s introduction in 2024, but it still isn’t universal. Lore Group and Capella participate, as do Anantara and many others. Titanium doesn’t guarantee club lounge access. And the ability to gift Titanium to someone else requires earning the status through the normal qualifying criteria so a match alone doesn’t get you that benefit. I’ve made several GHA Discovery stays through Amex Fine Hotels and Resorts as well as Chase’s The Edit, and benefits stack. At NH Collection Palazzo dei Dogi in Venice, early check-in and 4 p.m. checkout was especially useful. At Riggs in Washington, D.C., I booked through Chase’s The Edit and combined its benefits with GHA status. My suite was the former bank boardroom, with a dining table for twelve. I also combined American Express Fine Hotels + Resorts with GHA at Kempinski Cancun, receiving an oceanfront suite and club access. Greg’s Augustine Prague story was a good experience as well. He’d booked a hotel that converted to a Kempinski so he added his new GHA number and contacted the hotel. They combined the Fine Hotels + Resorts upgrade with Titanium’s double upgrade and put him in a historic Treasury suite. He also earned D$75 from the stay. Don’t Have The Bank Relationship? There’s Still A Paid Match I’ve covered GHA’s unusually broad status match offers before, including eligibility through airline and cruise status and selected credit cards rather than just another hotel program. The current paid match is scheduled to run through November 30, 2026, with status through December 31, 2027: Titanium costs $150 and comes with D$75. Platinum costs $100 and comes with D$50. The gift dollars expire after 12 months, and there isn’t a stay challenge required. Qualifying Titanium matches include Hilton Diamond, Hyatt Globalist, Marriott Platinum and above, and IHG Platinum and above, among others. For someone who will use all D$75, the Titanium offer has a $75 net cost. You can potentially match GHA Titanium onward to other programs as well. And the easiest way to qualify in some cities would be three one night stays at different brands.
